html:
A great Buddhist monastery and centre of learning in Magadha, in today's Bihar, India, that worked for some 800 years from the 5th century. It drew students from across Asia and is often called the world's first residential university.

It was founded in the 5th century; tradition credits the Gupta king Kumaragupta I. Later kings kept giving: Harsha in the 7th century, and the Pala Empire of Bengal from the 8th to the 12th. The site grew into a long row of brick monasteries and temples, with libraries housing thousands of manuscripts.

Monks studied Buddhist philosophy, especially the Mahayana schools, but also logic, grammar, medicine and the Vedas. Admission was said to be hard; gatekeepers quizzed applicants.

Foreign students made it famous:

  • Xuanzang of China studied there in the 630s and wrote a detailed description.
  • Yijing came in the 670s, after time in Srivijaya, and stayed about ten years.
  • Scholars from Nalanda took Buddhism to the Tibetan Empire in the 8th century, and Tibetan Buddhism still follows its traditions of debate and study.

Nalanda declined as Buddhism lost royal support in India. Around 1200 it was sacked by Turkish troops under Bakhtiyar Khalji, and its monks scattered; some teaching may have continued on a small scale for a while. The ruins were excavated from 1915 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. A new Nalanda University opened nearby in 2014.
sum: A great Buddhist monastery and centre of learning in Magadha, in today's Bihar, India, that worked for some 800 years from the 5th century. It drew students from across Asia and is often called the world's first residential university.
